pages.seo_title: House Construction Stages: A 14-Step Schedule | Buildiary
pages.title: The stages of building a house, from design to handover
pages.excerpt: The 14 stages of building a typical two-storey house in Pakistan and the Gulf, how long each takes, what depends on what, and what to check before moving on.
pages.lede: A typical two-storey family house moves through five phases (design, approval, grey structure, finishing and handover) in about 18 months. Here is the order of work most good builders follow, and what to check at each step.
blocks: The five phases at a glance
Brief, concept plans, then structural, electrical and plumbing drawings
Building plan approved by the authority or society
Excavation, foundation, columns, slabs, walls and plaster
Wiring and plumbing, tiles, woodwork, kitchen, paint and fittings
These times are typical for a two-storey house. Size, weather, approvals and, above all, cash flow make the real schedule shorter or longer.

Agree the rooms, sizes, style and budget with your architect. The concept plans fix the layout; every change after this point costs more. Check that the plans meet the plot's bylaws: setbacks, covered area and height.

The structural engineer designs the foundations, columns, beams and slabs. Electrical and plumbing drawings show every point, pipe and board. Check that the drawings are signed and that the quantities and contract are based on them.

Submit the drawings to the development authority or society (for example a DHA, Bahria Town, LDA, KDA or CDA) or, in Saudi Arabia, the municipality through Balady. Most authorities don't allow work to start without it. Keep the approved set on site and build to it.

The plot is cleared and marked out, a water supply, store and labour shelter are set up, and the ground is dug to the foundation level in the drawings. Check the layout against the approved plan before digging.

Lean concrete, footings and plinth beams are cast; anti-termite treatment and a damp-proof course protect the house from below. Check the steel before every pour and the plinth level before walls start.

Columns are cast, then the formwork and steel for the beams and roof slab, then the pour. Electrical conduits and pipe sleeves go in before the concrete. Use a slab checklist before pouring, and keep the slab wet for at least 7 days after.
The same cycle for the upper floor. The props under the slab stay until the structural engineer allows them to be removed.
8. Block masonry, parapet and water tanks

Walls are built in block or brick, with lintels over doors and windows; the parapet and the underground and overhead water tanks are built. Check that walls are plumb and openings are the right size, and test the tanks for leaks before plaster.
Inside and outside plaster, and roof insulation and waterproofing. The grey structure is now complete: measure it and settle the grey structure account before finishing starts.
10. Electrical and plumbing first fix, window frames
Wiring, boards, water and drain pipes, gas lines, and door and window frames go in before floors and tiles. Pressure-test the water pipes and photograph every pipe and wire run before it is covered.
Floors, bathroom and kitchen tiles, and stone. Check levels and the slope towards drains, use tiles from one batch, and keep a few spare boxes.
Doors, wardrobes, kitchen cabinets and aluminium or uPVC windows, alongside the tiling. Measure on site after plaster, not from the drawings.
Putty and paint, then taps, basins, toilets, lights, switches and fans. Check that every point works and nothing leaks under the basins.
Walk through every room with the builder and list every defect. The builder fixes them, then hands over the keys, drawings and warranties. Keep a small retention until the snags are fixed.

Some stages overlap and some cannot. Approval can run while the structural drawings are finished, and woodwork can run alongside tiling. But nothing structural should start before the drawings are approved, and finishing should not start until the grey structure is complete and settled.

When you start a project in Buildiary, these 14 stages are added for you and spread between your start and finish dates. Your team records progress against each stage with photos, so you always know where the work stands and what comes next.
faq: How long does it take to build a house in Pakistan?

A two-storey family house typically takes about 15 to 20 months from design to handover: around 8 months for the grey structure and 6 to 8 months for finishing. Approvals, cash flow and the size of the house change this.
What is grey structure?

The grey structure is the frame and shell of the building: foundations, columns, slabs, walls and plaster, without finishes. In Pakistan it is often given to one contractor and paid for separately from the finishing.
What is the difference between grey structure and finishing?

Grey structure is the shell. Finishing is everything that makes it a home: wiring and plumbing fittings, floors, tiles, woodwork, kitchen, paint and fixtures. Finishing often costs as much as the grey structure, or more, depending on the materials chosen.

pages.seo_title: Construction Material Control: Stop Loss on Site | Buildiary
pages.title: How to stop material going missing on a building site
pages.excerpt: Cement, steel, tiles and fittings are a large part of a house's cost. A simple routine (order, receive, store, release, reconcile) keeps them under control.
pages.lede: On most house builds, material is a large part of the cost, and it is where money quietly leaks: short deliveries, extra bags used, items that leave the site. You don't need a warehouse system to stop it, just a routine that every delivery and every release follows.
blocks: Short deliveries: 95 bags on a 100-bag delivery note, or steel lighter than billed.
Wrong quality: a cheaper brand or a thinner bar than ordered.
No record of use: bags released without anyone noting where they went.
Waste: mortar mixed and left to set, broken blocks, badly cut tiles.
Theft: material leaving the site after hours.
Every purchase starts with a written order: item, brand, size, quantity and rate. A delivery that doesn't match an order is questioned at the gate.
Count the bags, count or weigh the steel, and check the brand and size against the order. Photograph the supplier's delivery note and the load, and note who received it.
Keep cement dry and off the floor, in stacks no more than about 10 bags high, and use the oldest bags first. Keep fittings and small items locked. Make one person responsible for the store.
4. Release to a named person for a named job
Material leaves the store only to a named mistri or foreman, for a named piece of work: '20 bags to Akram for the first-floor columns'. Returns are recorded the same way.

Compare what was issued with what the work needed. For example, a 1:2:4 concrete mix uses roughly 6 to 7 bags of cement per cubic metre; your engineer can tell you what a pour should need. Count the store by surprise every few weeks.
What to check on common materials
Count the bags; check the brand, grade and packing date
Dry, on a raised platform, about 10 bags high at most; oldest first
Check diameter and grade; count or weigh against the bill
Off the ground, covered, sorted by size
Count by stacks; check the size and broken pieces
Stacked near the work, away from traffic
Measure the loaded truck (length × width × height) against the volume billed
In a marked area on hard ground
Check size, shade and batch on every box
Boxed, one batch together; keep spare boxes
Check model and quantity against the order
Where there is no mains water, water is bought by the tanker. Record each tanker's size, time and who received it, and check the tank levels, so you pay only for water that arrived.

Buildiary follows this routine on the phone. Goods are received against the purchase order with a photo of the delivery note, every release goes to a named person, stock is live, and low-stock alerts warn you before work stops. You can even find an item by taking its photo.
faq: How high can cement bags be stacked?
Keep stacks to about 10 bags high, on a dry raised platform away from the walls, and use the oldest bags first.
How do I check a sand or crush delivery?
Measure the truck's loaded length, width and height, multiply them, and compare the volume with what the supplier is charging for.
Who should keep the site store?
One trusted person, usually the store keeper or supervisor. Material should leave the store only through them, to a named person for a named job.

pages.seo_title: Construction Site Diary: What to Record Every Day | Buildiary
pages.title: How to keep a construction site diary that settles arguments
pages.excerpt: What a daily site diary should record (weather, people, work done, deliveries, instructions and problems) and why it protects owners and builders alike.
pages.lede: A site diary is the daily record of what happened on site. Good engineers have always kept one, because when there is a dispute about a delay, a payment or a defect, the diary is the evidence. It takes five minutes a day.
blocks: Date, weather and working hours, including rain or heat that stopped work
Who was on site: mistris and labour by trade, and any visitors
Work done, by location: 'first-floor slab steel fixed, east side'
Instructions given, and by whom, especially changes from the owner or architect
Inspections and tests, and their result
Problems: delays, accidents, shortages and defects
Photos of each of the above
Payments: claims for work done are backed by a dated record.
Delays: you can show which days were lost to rain, approvals or late material.
Quality: years later you can see when something was built and who was there.
Changes: spoken instructions become written ones.
Tips for a diary people actually keep
Make one person responsible, usually the supervisor.
Fill it in on site during the day, not from memory at night.
Prefer photos to long text: one photo with a caption beats a paragraph.
Let the owner and the builder read the same diary.
Never change old entries; add a correction instead.
Ground-floor roof: formwork and steel fixed; checked by the engineer
Received 200 bags of cement (delivery note 1452); released 30 bags for the stairs
Owner: move the kitchen window 300 mm to the left
Slab pour moved to Thursday: crush delivery late

In Buildiary the supervisor writes the day's diary on the phone, with photos. Deliveries, releases, attendance and inspections are recorded alongside it, so the owner sees the whole day in one place, in English, Urdu or Arabic.
faq: Who should keep the site diary?
The site supervisor or engineer, every day. The owner and the builder should both be able to read it.
Is a WhatsApp group enough as a site diary?
It helps, but messages get lost, are not organised by date or place, and can be deleted. A diary keeps the same facts in order, in one place.

pages.seo_title: How to Budget a House Build and Control Payments | Buildiary
pages.title: How to budget your house build and keep payments under control
pages.excerpt: Split the budget by phase, keep a contingency, decide finishes early, pay against work done and keep proof of every payment. A practical guide for home owners.
pages.lede: Most house builds go over budget in the same places: finishes chosen late, advances never adjusted, and small cash payments nobody added up. A budget by phase and a few payment rules prevent most of it.
blocks: Split the budget the way the work happens, then split each phase into its main items.
Architect, structural engineer, approval fees, soil test
Excavation, concrete, steel, blocks, plaster, labour, water
Electrical, plumbing, tiles, stone, woodwork, kitchen, aluminium, paint, fixtures
For the unexpected, commonly about 10% of the total

Finishing is where budgets slip, because choices are made late and one at a time. Choose the tiles, sanitary ware, kitchen and lights before the grey structure ends, price them, and put them in the budget.
Pay for work done and checked, not for time passed.
Keep advances small, and adjust them against the following bills.
Keep proof of every payment: a bill, a receipt or a transfer slip.
Hold back a small retention, often around 5%, until the snag list is cleared.
Give petty cash in small amounts, against receipts, and top it up weekly.
Compare what you have paid each supplier with what they delivered.
You buy the material; the contractor supplies the labour at a rate per square foot
Controlling material is your job: track every delivery and release
The contractor builds the grey structure at a rate per square foot, material included
Write down the brands, steel grade and concrete mix, and check them
One contractor builds and finishes the whole house at an agreed price
A clear specification for every finish, and payments tied to stages

Money is needed in waves: large payments for concrete and steel during the grey structure, then for tiles, woodwork and fittings during finishing. A month-by-month cash forecast shows when you need funds, so work doesn't stop while you wait for money.

Buildiary keeps the budget by phase, shows what is committed in orders and what has been paid, and forecasts the cash you will need month by month. Every payment carries its proof, and the owner approves petty cash.
faq: How much contingency should I keep when building a house?
Many owners keep about 10% of the total budget for the unexpected, and more if the design is not final.
Should I pay my contractor in advance?
A small mobilisation advance is common. Keep it small and adjust it against the following bills, so payments always follow work done.
What is retention in a construction contract?
A small part of each payment, often around 5%, held back until the snag list is cleared and the work is handed over.

pages.seo_title: Roof Slab Casting Checklist: Before, During, After | Buildiary
pages.title: Roof slab casting checklist: what to check before, during and after the pour
pages.excerpt: A roof slab can't be fixed after it sets. Check the formwork, steel, cover, services and concrete before you pour, and cure the slab properly afterwards.
pages.lede: A roof slab is poured in a day and lasts for decades. Most slab problems, such as cracks, sagging, exposed steel and leaks, come from something that could have been checked before the concrete arrived. Go through this list with your engineer.
blocks: Shuttering level and at the right height; props on firm ground, braced and evenly spaced
Joints tight, so cement slurry doesn't leak out
Formwork clean and oiled, with no wood chips, wire or standing water
Openings for stairs, ducts and skylights in the right place
Bar sizes and spacing as in the structural drawing
Laps as long as the drawing specifies, and staggered
Cover blocks under the bottom bars and at the edges, at the cover in the drawing (often about 20 to 25 mm for slabs)
Top bars held up on chairs so they are not pressed down
Steel clean: no mud, oil or loose rust
Beam and column steel tied in as drawn
Electrical conduits and boxes fixed, joints taped
Sleeves for plumbing and drainage through the slab
Fan hooks and anchor points in place
Everything photographed, because it will soon be covered
The mix as specified (for example 1:2:4, or a ready-mix grade), with no extra water added to make it flow
Concrete vibrated, especially around the steel and at beam joints
Poured continuously, without long stops that leave cold joints
Test cubes taken, if your engineer asks for them
Once the surface has set, keep the slab wet for at least 7 days, longer in hot, dry weather
Make small mortar ponds and keep them filled, or cover the slab with wet hessian
No heavy loads or stacked material on the new slab
Leave the props until your engineer says they can be removed

Buildiary's inspections turn a checklist like this into a few taps on site, with a photo for each check. Problems become snags with a person and a due date, and the owner sees the result before the pour goes ahead.
faq: How long should a roof slab be cured?
Keep it wet for at least 7 days after it sets, and longer in hot, dry weather. Ponding with small mortar bunds is the usual method on house sites.
When can the props under a slab be removed?
Only when your structural engineer allows it. It depends on the span, the concrete and the weather; for house slabs it is often around two weeks.
Can water be added to concrete to make it easier to pour?
No. Extra water weakens the concrete. If the mix is too stiff, ask your engineer; a well-designed mix is workable without it.
